name: GDPR Procedural Regulation
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: no IA or indicators; baseline figures and opposing expert opinions; applies from 2027
summary: The GDPR Procedural Regulation was adopted without an impact assessment or monitoring indicators, aiming to speed up cross-border data protection cases that often take years. It only applies to cases opened from April 2027, so there is no evidence yet on whether it works. Regulators backed it, while privacy campaigners warned the final text may be too complex to deliver faster decisions.

indicators.objective: No impact assessment and no LFS indicators: the memorandum says only that the Commission will monitor the Regulation together with the GDPR. The Regulation applies to cross-border cases opened after 2 April 2027.
Faster cross-border GDPR enforcement and quicker remedies for individuals
indicators.indicator: Duration of cross-border investigations; number of disputes sent to the EDPB
indicators.evidence: Baseline only (Commission 2nd GDPR report, data to Nov 2023): ~2,400 cross-border case entries; ~1,500 lead-authority draft decisions, 990 final infringement decisions; median complaint handling 1-12 months across authorities. No post-application data.

indicators.objective: Harmonised complaint admissibility and procedural rights for complainants and parties
indicators.evidence: Not measured. Critics (noyb) argued the trilogue text created many procedure types and could lengthen cases; no evidence either way yet.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Second Report on the application of the General Data Protection Regulation, COM(2024) 357
literature.title: Second Report on the application of the General Data Protection Regulation
literature.headline: Almost 2,400 cross-border case entries; ~1,500 draft decisions, 990 final infringement decisions (Nov 2023); DPAs receive 100,000+ complaints a year; calls for swift adoption of the procedural rules proposal to deliver quick remedies
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's 2024 GDPR review described slow, uneven cross-border enforcement and urged adoption of the procedural rules to speed it up.

literature.citation: EDPB & EDPS (2023), Joint Opinion 01/2023 on the Proposal for a Regulation laying down additional procedural rules relating to the enforcement of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion, September 2023
literature.title: Joint Opinion 01/2023 on the Proposal for a Regulation laying down additional procedural rules relating to the enforcement of Regulation (EU) 2016/679
literature.headline: Welcomes harmonised complaint admissibility and streamlining of cooperation; calls for swift adoption; stresses complainants' procedural rights
literature.summary_plain: Europe's data protection regulators backed the proposal as a way to speed up cross-border cases, while asking for stronger rights for complainants.
literature.interested_party: The regulators who apply the rules (the proposal followed the EDPB's own 2022 wish list)

literature.citation: Euronews (reporting noyb) (2025), EU plans to reform data protection rules are 'tangled mess', privacy advocates warn, Euronews, 18 April 2025
literature.title: EU plans to reform data protection rules are 'tangled mess', privacy advocates warn
literature.headline: noyb argued the trilogue draft would create around ten types of GDPR procedure and could lengthen investigations; Max Schrems called it 'the biggest legislative mess I have seen in a long time'
literature.summary_plain: Privacy group noyb warned that the negotiated text was so complex it could slow, rather than speed up, cross-border GDPR enforcement.
literature.interested_party: noyb files many cross-border GDPR complaints
